metaData.originalTitle: Building a Secure MCP Server on AWS for a Million-Company B2B Platform
metaData.title: Building a Secure MCP Server on AWS for a Million-Company B2B Platform
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents a production-grade approach to building a secure MCP server on AWS for a B2B platform with over one million company profiles, emphasizing read/write separation, default-deny mutations, narrow tool contracts, and rigorous testing strategies.
metaData.summary: This article details the design and implementation of a secure MCP (Model Context Protocol) server on AWS, built to expose a B2B intelligence platform with over one million company profiles to LLM clients. The authors treat the MCP server as a first-class production interface, not a thin demo wrapper. Key architectural decisions include strict separation of read and write operations at the tool level, a default-deny approach to mutations enforced via a `--allow-mutations` flag, and the use of narrow, well-defined tool contracts with bounded input and output structures. The server, built in Go, uses GraphQL on AWS AppSync as its backend and authenticates via short-lived OIDC tokens. The article also covers a comprehensive testing strategy combining mocked unit tests with real-system validation through MCP Inspector, which uncovered a critical backend Lambda null-pointer error that unit tests missed. The authors argue that for production systems, tool contracts, validation layers, and operational controls matter more than the protocol itself.

mainPoints.point: MCP servers should be designed as production interfaces with their own contracts, not as thin wrappers around existing APIs.
mainPoints.explanation: Treating the MCP layer as a first-class interface with explicit validation, security, and testing strategies prevents it from becoming an unsafe bridge between an LLM and production data.

mainPoints.point: Separating read and write operations at the tool level is a simple and effective risk reduction strategy.
mainPoints.explanation: Read-only tools are simpler to test, review, and observe. Mutation-capable tools are gated by a `--allow-mutations` flag, forcing a deliberate decision before write paths are enabled.

mainPoints.point: Narrow, well-defined tool contracts are more important than the number of tools.
mainPoints.explanation: Nine narrowly scoped tools with clear input models and bounded output structures are safer and more maintainable than two general-purpose ones, especially when dealing with probabilistic LLM clients.

mainPoints.point: A comprehensive testing strategy requires both mocked unit tests and real-system validation.
mainPoints.explanation: Mocked tests caught normalization bugs like incorrect country-code resolution, but only real-system validation through MCP Inspector revealed a backend Lambda null-pointer error that unit tests missed.

mainPoints.point: Authentication should be user-specific and short-lived, not based on static credentials.
mainPoints.explanation: Using OIDC bearer tokens tied to individual users ensures that the MCP server inherits the platform's existing authorization model and audit trails, while short-lived tokens limit the blast radius of a compromised credential.

keyQuotes: MCP servers should be designed as production interfaces, not as thin demo wrappers around existing APIs.
Separating read and write operations at the tool level is one of the simplest and most effective ways to reduce risk in LLM-connected systems.
A default-deny approach to mutations creates a safer path from experimentation to production use.
Tool contracts matter more than tool count.
The most important production failure in the project was not caught by unit tests... This situation is why real-system validation through MCP Inspector remained a release gate.
